Unlocking the Hidden Doors Inside the Biltmore Estate

However some of the estate’s most fascinating features are hidden, intentionally tucked away, designed as much for beautiful aesthetics as they were to accommodate hospitality.

These concealed doors and passageways were built to allow Vanderbilt’s guests to move about more freely between corridors, or simply hide the behind-the-scenes hustle and bustle of the staff’s daily chores.

The Winter Garden is the room where tropical plants would have been located, surviving even during the harsh winter months. Underneath this vast, marble floor was the potted plant room located in the subbasement. Servants would use these large, heavy trap doors, which are concealed in the same marble flooring, to bring the potted plants up to the main level, eliminating the need to carry the plants through visible guest areas.

Early plans indicate an elevator was supposed to be installed under the trap doors, however one never was and a ladder remains in its place. If you peek down into the trap doors, you’ll see that the potted plant room has now been replaced by an employee break room.

Vanderbilt’s Billiard Room has an elaborate hidden wooden door concealed into the wall which leads to the gentlemen’s Smoking Room. Guests could open the door with the push of a button that released the lock holding the door in place. The Billiard Room was used for billiards and tabletop games such as dominoes.

Although it was primarily a gentleman’s room, it was also occasionally used by women. The concealed Smoking Room was much more exclusive, however. It was mostly the gentlemen’s domain, where Vanderbilt and his guests would retire with brandy and cigars.

The Breakfast Room was used as the informal dining room, although by today’s standards, it’s not very informal. With two Renoir portraits hanging on the wall, "Young Algerian Girl" and "Child with an Orange,” it’s certainly a fancier setting than what a typical family is used to in 2015. The “Child with an Orange” portrait is actually hanging on the hidden door, which leads into the Butler’s Pantry.

If you look closely you can see the doorknob below the frame on the right to allow servants to enter discreetly with hot meals. Hand-tooled Spanish leather and red Italian marble adjoin the walls, which is the same material used to cover the hidden doorway to create a seamless appearance.

The Biltmore Estate’s stunning library holds more than 10,000 books, many of which are first editions. The library is two stories tall, with a spiral staircase leading up to a balcony that extends behind the fireplace to the other side of the room. A door located on the balcony leads to a secret passageway outside of Vanderbilt’s guest’s bedrooms on the second floor. This was designed to allow guests to go back and forth from their rooms to grab a book without having to travel all the way down the grand staircase and back.

For instance, a lady could grab a book in her nightgown and quickly get back to her room, something that would not have been permissible down the grand staircase in the highly-trafficked area of the Estate.

Vanderbilt’s closet door is covered in burlap with a gold leaf on top. He took great care in every detail of the architecture in the Biltmore Estate, even concealing the closet doors in certain rooms, such as his own. This was to avoid the break in symmetry that a doorframe would create.

Secrets of the Biltmore Estate

Biltmore’s immensity is matched only by the thoughtfulness and attention to detail of the three men responsible for its design and construction: George Vanderbilt, architect Richard Morris Hunt, and landscape designer Frederick Law Olmsted.

While land acquisition began in earnest that year same year, Vanderbilt hired Hunt, an accomplished architect responsible for a handful of Vanderbilt residences in the Northeast. Vanderbilt and Hunt traveled together to England and France to gather design inspiration, paying particular attention to Waddesdon Manor in Buckinghamshire and several sixteenth-century chateaux in the Loire Valley.

With a dairy farm, a railway station, a church, and a school, the estate functioned as a self-supporting agrarian village.

In 1898, three years after moving in at Biltmore, George married Edith Stuyvesant Dresser. Their daughter, Cornelia, was born in 1900. George Vanderbilt died suddenly in 1914, leaving his wife and young daughter to shoulder the burden of the enormous estate and the livelihoods of those who depended upon it.

Edith and Cornelia survived by selling portions of the land surrounding the estate and continued to run Biltmore Farms at a profit. Cornelia’s son, William A.V. Cecil, transformed Biltmore from a struggling private home to a self-sustaining tourist attraction in the mid-twentieth century.

If it’s a slower day in the third floor living hall, ask the host to see a reproduction copy of a book published in 1883 called Mr. Vanderbilt’s House and Collection. It includes detailed interior shots of the demolished Fifth Avenue mansion, and you can easily spot the pieces saved and brought to Biltmore.

Underground Asheville: Exploring passages, purpose beneath city

Oct 28, 2015

On a chilly fall day during leaf season, Pack's Tavern is crowded with tourists at lunchtime. But below, in the depths of the basement, is a big secret.

Or, it could just be a vault.

On the lower floor of the restaurant space is a dark tunnel, or the fragment of one really, and like many pieces of underground Asheville, it's rumored to be a part of a subterranean web of passageways which had possibly nefarious purposes.

Vance Pollock, Asheville historian and frequent right-hand man to local occult expert Joshua P. Warren, said there's enough evidence to support the notion that underground Asheville existed.

And behind steel doors at Pack's Tavern is one piece of that puzzle.

"It helps lend credibility to some of the more mysterious rumors and outrageous claims," said Pollock, who with Warren runs the Asheville Mystery Museum in the basement of the Asheville Masonic Temple as well as Haunted Asheville tours. "But criminal activity, prostitution and bootlegging ties in with that."

Indeed, Pack's Tavern managers and owners will tell you that the Spruce Street building, which incorporates two structures built between 1907 and 1912, was a center of illegal liquor smuggling during the Prohibition years via the underground passageway, now bricked off at the rear but still guarded by steel doors with locks inside and out.

Pollock, who claims the tunnel used to lead directly to the police station, said the cops were allegedly some of the biggest bootleggers.

"The police would raid a still or barroom and take all the illegal liquor downstairs to what would be the evidence room, impound it, and smuggle it through Westall's Lumber, which is now Pack's Tavern, into the police station never to be seen again," he said.

As for where the rest of Asheville's tunnels led, or for what purpose they were created, it's hard to say for sure. "I think they were mainly utility; certainly, they were there at least early after World War I, and I have evidence of some of those places," Pollock said.

But in 2010, Pollock and Warren spent months digging up research to produce the Underground Asheville Tour, a short-lived endeavor that failed as a business, but uncovered the likelihood that original maintenance and drainage tunnels were long ago expanded into experimental tunnels for a subway.

"However, we never found an official document to state this," Warren said in an email from Puerto Rico, where he lives for part of the year. "It would make sense, considering the streetcars were viewed as a nuisance in those days when the lanes of Asheville were packed with pedestrians."

Warren thinks the tunnel network downtown had a rough V-shape, with the crux of the V around Pack's Tavern, the left-hand side running past the monument and down Patton Avenue toward Church Street, with the other connecting to what is now Rat Alley, the alleyway adjacent to Wall Street which now serves as a space for restaurant dumpsters.

Pollock thinks Rat Alley is just that — an alley.

But for the rest of Asheville's shadowy network of tunnels, he said it makes sense that Prohibition would push the knowledge of those tunnels into the realm of privileged information. Nothing dampens the mood of a smuggling more than a sightseer.

Another shady secret has it that a tunnel used to lead to a brothel below the Langren Hotel. "But when the hotel was demolished, so were the tunnel spaces," Warren said.

Where's the proof? Well, according to Warren, it's a Homeland Security issue for any city to provide information regarding underground infrastructure.

A sketch showing plans for the old City Hall site, including plans for underground walkways, which historian Vance Pollock thinks would have connected to service passageways shown on old blueprints of subterranean bathrooms under Pack Square.

Yet old-timers with the water department claim an extensive tunnel system ran down Charlotte Street, he said, with an entrance now buried under center-field at the Martin Luther King ballpark.

But city improvement has rendered any tunnels that might have existed into mostly a hodgepodge of disconnected spaces, many existing as storage spaces below restaurants and other businesses, some of which have their own colorful stories. Warren and Pollock will tell you a section of tunnel below the now-defunct Vincenzo's was used to store excess corpses during the Spanish Flu epidemic of 1918. "But if you go down there now, you can just peek through a hole in the wall, into the space they say was once used," Warren said.

And according to Warren, in 2010 you could go into the bathroom at the Sisters McMullen Cupcake Corner, where Bomba now is, and find a door on the floor. "If you lifted it and climbed down a ladder, you would find yourself in a sizable chunk of the underground system," he said. "They were using it as storage at the time."

Additionally, Warren, himself a Mason, is fond of saying that he can neither "confirm nor deny" the existence of another tunnel below the Asheville Masonic Temple.

But for Pollock's part, he's never seen it. But he has studied the blueprints of the subterranean bathrooms under Pack Square, now covered with a concrete slab and sealed off until about a decade ago, when the last major renovation of the Pack Square area busted into the bathrooms.

As proof, Pollock proffered a Xeroxed copy of the blueprints, which seem to show service tunnels leading away from them and to the north and south.

Although many such tunnels were used for service-related affairs, their mysterious nature has given them the reputation for having more sinister uses.

"If it's out of eyesight of people, they'll automatically assume the worst," said Pollock. "Tales of murder and law-breaking and organized crime."

That's not so say that the worst didn't sometimes happen.

In the Jackson Underground, a downtown deli in the basement of the Jackson Building, are old black-and-white photos that show the old domed City Hall, which sat in front of the current City Hall site before being torn down in the 20s.

That building contained a basement level housing the fire department as well as some underground chambers where, according to Pollock, some unsavory things did happen.

That includes a 1900 incident when Asheville Police Chief J.A. Lyerly dragged an unruly prisoner from the 1st-floor jail cells to what was called "the dungeon" at the time.

The Asheville Register reported that the prisoner attacked the chief, who then found a pick-handle nearby with which he violently bludgeoned the prisoner to death in the basement of City Hall.

"It was found that the skull had been fractured for a considerable length on the right side, fragments of the bone being driven into the brain causing congestion and paralysis," the Register reported. "He never recovered consciousness and died in about three hours after the fight."

"Absolutely, some violent things happened underground in the immediate downtown," Pollock remarked.

Back at Pack's Tavern, marketing and events manager Mary Evans threw open the steel doors to reveal what remained of the rumored tunnel, a section walled off in the rear, with doors that lock from both the inside and out, evidence that sneaky behavior took place within, according to Pollock.

Though some claim that what now looks like a subterranean storage closet was only a vault, he added.

But Evans said the stories she's heard are consistent with Pollock's claim of liquor smuggling by police. "It's a much better story than a vault, anyway," she said.

But when others have tried to drill into the concrete at the back of the space, stagnant water rushed in through the holes, hampering progress.

An unsolvable mystery? "It's definitely peculiar," said Pollock.
